item.title: When Good Things Go Wrong in Love
item.description:
Relationships

When Good Things Go Wrong in Love

How romantic virtues become liabilities.

Posted August 8, 2026

Key points
  • Sexual desire strengthens love when integrated with commitment and self-control.
  • Sacrifice benefits relationships when voluntary, reciprocal, and limited.
  • Patience supports love but should not excuse persistent mistreatment.

Romantic love draws upon some of our finest qualities: kindness, friendship, patience, generosity, openness, wisdom, sexual desire, and a willingness to sacrifice for another person. Yet love is also vulnerable to infidelity, selfishness, jealousy, and emotional hurt. How can such admirable virtues coexist with love's darker tendencies? And can virtues themselves sometimes become part of the problem?

We often assume that if a quality is good, more of it must be better. Yet this is rarely true in human life, and especially not in romantic life. A virtue that enriches a relationship in moderation may damage it when expressed without limits, balance, or wisdom. Here, I examine three romantic virtues—sexual desire, sacrifice, and patience—and argue that each can contribute to flourishing love, but each can also become harmful when taken to an extreme.

Too Much Sexual Desire

"Love is a fire. But whether it is going to warm your hearth or burn down your house, you can never tell." —Joan Crawford

sexual desire
Source: Cottonbro / Pexels

Sexual desire is often compared to a raging fire. Both are described as intense, swift, and potentially insatiable. Fire and sexual desire have constructive as well as destructive aspects; in both cases, the difference between warmth and disaster may depend on how intensity is managed. A strong fire can warm a house, but it can also burn it down. Similarly, intense sexual desire can enrich romantic love, but when it becomes obsessive or difficult to regulate, it can undermine the relationship and, in some cases, resemble an addiction. When integrated into a broader emotional bond, sexual desire can deepen intimacy, pleasure, and romantic connection.

The spontaneous nature of sexual desire does not mean that it is entirely immune to learning, habits, or social conventions. People can sometimes learn to cultivate sexual attraction toward their partners, just as they can develop strategies for managing or reducing sexual impulses.

The lesson is not that strong sexual desire is bad. Rather, sexual desire serves love best when it is integrated with commitment, self-control, and consideration for the beloved. Even a powerful romantic virtue can become destructive when it dominates the relationship.

Too Much Sacrifice

"A thing is not necessarily true because a man dies for it." —Oscar Wilde

When we sacrifice, we give up something meaningful in order to obtain or preserve something else. Romantic sacrifices involve giving up a significant non-romantic value for romantic reasons—for example, devoting less time to one's work in order to spend more time with a beloved. At its best, sacrifice is a voluntary choice that goes beyond what duty requires.

article continues after advertisement

Close relationships inevitably involve situations requiring sacrifice because partners have different desires, interests, and values. These conflicts may be minor, such as choosing a restaurant, or major, such as deciding whether to have another child or where to live. Two common ways of dealing with such conflicts are sacrifice and compromise.

Many people regard sacrifice as an expression of genuine love. In close relationships, willingness to sacrifice is associated with greater relationship satisfaction and stability. People often interpret sacrifice as evidence of caring, trust, respect, and loyalty. Willingness to sacrifice can therefore strengthen security and reinforce the sense that the relationship matters.

Sacrifice can also benefit the person who makes it. Giving to a partner may strengthen self-respect, deepen gratitude, and encourage reciprocity. In this sense, generous giving can benefit both partners.

Yet sacrifice has limits. It can become harmful when it is excessive, chronic, or one-sided. Problems arise when one partner repeatedly gives up important personal goals, values, or desires for the sake of the other, particularly when the sacrifice is not reciprocated. In unequal relationships, the less powerful partner may be especially likely to sacrifice, sometimes while suppressing or "silencing" their own opinions and desires.

Healthy sacrifice says, "I am willing to give something up for us." Unhealthy sacrifice says, "I must give myself up for you." The first can deepen love; the second can gradually destroy the self that love is supposed to nurture.

Too Much Patience

"Perhaps there is only one cardinal sin: impatience. Because of impatience we were driven out of Paradise; because of impatience we cannot return." —W. H. Auden

Patience involves the ability to endure waiting, difficulties, or frustration without becoming excessively annoyed or upset. Passion, by contrast, involves excitement, intensity, and a tendency to experience emotions strongly. Profound romantic love requires both qualities: the excitement of passion and the calmness that allows love to endure over time (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019).

article continues after advertisement

The heart is often impatient with matters that seem to have merely superficial or extrinsic value. When something does not matter deeply to us, we want to achieve our goal as quickly as possible and are reluctant to invest unnecessary time and effort.

In profound love, however, there may be less need to rush. When we are deeply satisfied with our relationship, waiting can become tolerable, and even meaningful. The general mood of a patient heart is one of calm and peaceful joy. For the impatient heart, distance and delay may be intolerable. For the patient heart, temporary distance need not threaten togetherness.

Yet here too, patience has limits. Being patient does not mean accepting everything a beloved does. Patience toward temporary difficulties can sustain love; patience toward persistent disrespect, betrayal, or abuse can undermine it. Indeed, excessive tolerance may sometimes signal not wisdom but fear, dependency, or a lack of boundaries. As one married woman put it, "I would not call my behavior tolerant, as I was not tolerant toward my lover when he behaved in a wrong way (from my perspective). I love him too much to manifest tolerance."

This apparent paradox is important. Deep love does not necessarily make us more tolerant of everything our beloved does. Because the relationship matters so much, some behaviors may matter more, not less. Patience is therefore a romantic virtue, but not an unlimited one.

Our contemporary culture can make patience particularly difficult. We are accustomed to quick rewards and immediate gratification, from instant coffee to instant communication and, increasingly, expectations of instant romantic fulfillment. Yet love rarely develops according to the timetable of a smartphone.

The Limits of Virtue in Romantic Life

"I never promised you a rose garden; along with the sunshine, there's gotta be a little rain sometimes." —Joe South

The complexity of romantic love means that seemingly opposing tendencies often need to coexist. We desire our beloved intensely while exercising restraint. We sacrifice for the relationship while preserving our individuality. We practice patience while maintaining clear boundaries. Love flourishes not through the triumph of one virtue over another, but through their delicate balance.

article continues after advertisement

This raises an important question: If virtues are valuable, why should they ever be limited? One answer is that flourishing relationships require not only reducing vice but also regulating virtue. A virtue pursued without proportion can undermine the very good it is meant to serve.

Sexual desire, sacrifice, patience (and other virtues) are all valuable qualities. Yet none is universally beneficial in unlimited amounts. Their value depends upon context, timing, degree, and their relationship to other important values.

The central issue, therefore, is not whether a quality is good, but when it is good, how much of it is good, and how it fits within the broader fabric of a relationship. This is one of the deepest paradoxes of romantic life: the very qualities that help love flourish can, when unchecked, contribute to its decline.

A flourishing relationship requires more than passion, generosity, or patience. It requires practical wisdom—the capacity to recognize when a virtue has reached its appropriate limit. In love, as in life, the challenge is not simply to cultivate virtue, but to cultivate it in the right measure.

item.title: Why We Can’t Look Away From Perez Hilton’s Meltdown
item.description:
Self-Harm

Why We Can’t Look Away From Perez Hilton’s Meltdown

The science of morbid curiosity.

Posted August 8, 2026

Key points
  • Disturbing footage like Hilton's self-harm live-stream may activate the reward centers of our brain.
  • Emotional activation, novelty, and the desire to understand so as to protect ourselves increase the allure.
  • Morbid curiosity is common, but people high in neuroticism and anxiety tend to be more morbidly curious.

On Tuesday, August 4, 2026, blogger Perez Hilton live-streamed a brutal episode of self-mutilation for approximately 15 minutes on TikTok Live. The stream may have continued had the platform not taken the deeply disturbing content down earlier—though 15 minutes was an astonishingly long time for content that violated TIkTok’s policies to remain in place. (TikTok has since blamed technical challenges for the delay in shutting down the horrific stream.)

Thanks to “multiple calls regarding an individual who was live-streaming acts of self-harm,” Hilton was apprehended by Miami-Dade County police and transported to a hospital by emergency medical services.

Viewers of the livestream describe it as traumatizing. “I saw about two seconds of it and wanted to vomit,” wrote one Reddit user. Another commented that it was so disturbing as to trigger their own relapse of self-harm.

And yet. Some people are still seeking out the video, if not images from it or news about it. Why? What could possibly be compelling so many people to seek out such a disturbing and, for some, triggering video and story?

The Science of Morbid Curiosity

Disturbing content kicks off a series of neuropsychological responses apart from mere aversion. One of those responses involves the brain circuitry of reward. A 2020 fMRI study found that opting to consume violent content provoked a stronger activation of the striatum, inferior frontal gyrus, anterior cingulate cortex, and anterior insula—several regions involved in processing reward—when compared to opting for neutral or pleasant content.

Disturbing material may be more rewarding because it’s more emotionally activating as well as taboo—and what’s more alluring than the very thing we’re told not to think about, look at, or do? As study authors Suzanne Oosterwijk et al. explain, “negative information may be more novel, rare, deviant, uncertain, challenging or complex”—all of which engages reward circuitry through evoking curiosity and intrigue.

Add to this that upsetting material is more emotionally activating than non-upsetting material and this adds another layer of unfortunate magnetism to horrific imagery and news. It’s much harder not to read about, watch, or consume content that makes us feel something, even if that something is pretty horrified.

As researchers Coltan Scrivner and Joseph M. Stubbersfield note in their 2023 study on morbid curiosity, a huge pull of disturbing content is also the potential it has to help us learn from its threatening information. While much of the searching for news and images about Perez Hilton’s meltdown may stem from an irresistible urge to witness the terrifying, another motivation may be to better understand what the heck happened so that we and those we love can circumvent a similar fate.

Reward ≠ Pleasure

The pursuit of reward doesn’t always equate with peace or happiness. Reward seeking can sometimes be upsetting and anxiety-inducing. Drug-seeking is one example. Another is rumination, which can activate reward pathways but is anything but pleasant or good for us. See also: compulsive checking or reassurance seeking—they initially feel rewarding and activate many of the same reward processing structures due to temporary relief. But they ultimately perpetuate misery by preventing those who engage in them from tolerating uncertainty and trusting themselves, while often pushing others away.

It may make more sense, then, why many people couldn't look away from Hilton’s self-harm live-stream. They didn't enjoy it. They just couldn't help themselves.

Are Some People More Morbidly Curious than Others?

Morbid curiosity is a rather universal affliction. Research by Oosterwijk and Scrivner suggests that “general morbid curiosity appears to be a common behaviour and the trait has been found to be normally distributed in samples.” That said, some demographics tend to be higher in morbid curiosity than others.

Individuals who exhibit much higher degrees of morbid curiosity (think: those who are frantically searching for disturbing footage, chronically consume horror movies, and obsess over true crime) “tend to be younger, more rebellious, more socially curious, and less disgusted by or afraid of death,” as Scrivner and Stubbersfield explain. They also tend to be higher in anxiety and neuroticism than folks who more readily turn down invitations to gawk at the macabre. “This seemingly paradoxical finding could be explained by the heightened vigilance in morbidly curious people, which motivates them to seek out and attend to threat-related information.”

What to Do About Morbid Curiosity

While morbid curiosity can be normal to an extent, left unchecked it may negatively affect our mood and behavior by populating our minds with unforgettably disturbing content that colors our sense of safety and security. If you're finding it difficult to resist urges to look up or consume content that leaves you feeling worse, a good strategy is to set a timer for at least 20 minutes and take a media break. During that time, do something physical (ideally outside if you can) to shift your attention.

Another helpful (and science-backed) strategy is the Three Good Things exercise:

Scan the past 12-24 hours for three good things. They needn't be massive. A satisfying cup of coffee or pleasant smile from a stranger can do the trick. Just get to three. Re-live every single one in detail. Remember what you did to make each happen. Who else was involved? What time of day was it? What did that good thing do for you? How did you feel? The more effort we put into focusing on the good things, the more positive sentiment we foster and the more power we wrestle away from the negative information we've been exposed to.

If you or someone you love is self-harming or contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: The Unfragile Mind
item.description:
Psychiatry

The Unfragile Mind

A call for more hope and humanity in mental health care.

Posted August 8, 2026

Key points
  • Mental health is getting worse in the West, by the terms we use to measure it.
  • The rise is due to many complex interacting factors, and we in the therapeutic professions are implicated too.
  • States of mind are not rigid categories but dimensions of being.

Between a quarter and a fifth of young people in the UK now suffer a mental disorder by psychiatrists’ criteria, and over a half of young people say they have or have in the past suffered a mental disorder. One in six adults in America is prescribed psychiatric medication. These statistics represent a huge and relatively recent shift in how our society thinks about problems of thinking, feeling and being; it’s clear that, in Western society, by the terms with which we currently define it, our mental health is getting worse. I work as a general practitioner in the UK, and around 90% of clinical encounters to manage mental ill-health take place not in hospitals or with specialist psychiatrists, but with doctors in the community like myself. Between a third and a half of my consultations touch on mental illness.

Many factors have influenced this shift, and because so much discussion of it takes place online, opinion about causes has become polarised. One view is that the rise is due to a welcome and long-overdue recognition of just how widespread mental and emotional difficulties are in our culture, and that historic underfunding of mental health services has hugely contributed to our worsening health. Another is that as a society and in the therapeutic professions we are labelling normal feelings as pathological. Yet another view holds that the competitive, relentless pressures of our increasingly digital culture combined with a sluggish economy are making us ill. If you look for it, you can find elements of truth in all of these perspectives. In my clinical work, I don't get to choose a 'side' in these discussions; the perspectives and preoccupations my patients bring to the consulting room are the ones I have to work with. My responsibility with each remains the same: first, do no harm, then attempt to ease suffering.

I often have to reassure my patients that the categories in the DSM and the ICD are not drawn from neuroscience; they arise from culture and society – the life of the mind is inextricably cultural. The metaphor of ‘wiring’ in the brain has gone too far – our minds are a whirlpool, roiling and fluid, and nothing like a circuitboard. Archaeologists tell us that the human brain hasn’t changed much in size or shape in over 300,000 years, yet attitudes and approaches to the life of the mind shift relentlessly across time and geography – which is a reason for hope, because it means they can always change for the better. Our states of mind are experienced in context, and respond to flows of care and trauma, trust and distrust, love and disgust. The West’s overmedicalised discourse too often neglects the truth obvious to everyone with training in psychology: that mental health problems are dimensional, rather than categorical – which is to say that almost every issue is an exaggeration or a warping of a tendency that in a more measured dose, or a different context, could contribute to human wellbeing rather than detract from it.

The first ethical principle of medicine is ‘Do No Harm’, but there’s gathering evidence that some mental health diagnoses can sometimes do a great deal of harm – that they can become self-fulfilling spells that curse as often as they cure. The thresholds to be offered a diagnosis are much lower today than they were thirty years ago, and the range of feelings and behaviours that can be accorded a label are wider too. Mental health awareness campaigns have helped to destigmatise mental ill-health, but worrying evidence is also emerging that such campaigns sometimes worsen mental health outcomes. As the statistics for mental illness continue to move in the wrong direction, we in the therapeutic professions have to pause and take stock.

article continues after advertisement

We can’t blame all of the shift on the economy, or politicians, or social media, or Big Pharma, or Covid – we should ask how much we ourselves in the therapeutic professions are to blame. The statistics suggest that our mental health has become fragile, but our minds are not brittle or rigid, they are dynamic, resilient and adaptive – I’d say they’re better described as unfragile. Their capacity for change and growth is part of their very nature.

Other cultures do things differently, and haven’t seen such huge increases in mental ill-health in recent years. A kinder and more humble approach to psychiatry would be open to asking why that might be, and why our culture seems to be getting this so wrong. It’s time to recharge the public conversation around mental health and illness with a little more humility and curiosity. We need courage to discuss these issues openly, and the belief that as a society and as a therapeutic culture, we can do better.

item.title: Elephant-Human Conflicts: Enabling Practical Coexistence
item.description:
Environment

Elephant-Human Conflicts: Enabling Practical Coexistence

Dr. Nitin Sekar writes about the realities of sharing space with giants.

Posted August 8, 2026

Key points
  • A new book covers elephants and poverty, democracy, and the limits of good intentions in a complex world.
  • Conservation involves humility and trade-offs and is about enriching all our lives, human and non-human.
  • Win-wins for humans and nonhumans require investment.
A heartwarming scene of a mother and baby elephant in the wild, Thailans.
Source: Katie Hollamby/Pexels.

Elephants are sentient beings well-known for their incredible memory, intelligence, and rich emotional lives. In modern times, they come into conflict with neighboring humans, sometimes leading to fatalities. However, peaceful coexistence is a viable alternative, and for this and other reasons I found conservationist Dr. Nitin Sekar's highly acclaimed book, The Elephant Jungle: A Story of Conservation and Coexistence, to be a wonderful read about the lives of the people who are the guardians of India’s remaining wildlife.

In his easy-to-read book, Sekar offers grounded insights about how to achieve coexistence in a "crowded and complex world." He presents an important case study about compassionate conservation in which the well-being of all stakeholders matter, with global implications about the complexity of human-animal relationships.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write The Elephant Jungle?

Nitin Sekar: The Elephant Jungle centers on the life story of Netra Sharma, a villager I worked with closely during my research in Buxa Tiger Reserve, India. The book uses our stories to show the difficulties faced by both low-income farmers and megafauna when they're expected to share a landscape.

My real reason for writing the book is that Netra's story—of protecting wildlife in a place where people still faced desperate poverty, even when many valued animal life—was extremely interesting. I couldn't let it go until I wrote the book.

More cerebrally: I started my PhD in ecology thinking that understanding how animals affected their ecosystems was core to conservation. In the field, I found a different reality—one where the factors shaping decisions in Buxa had to do with the economic, social, and political relationships of local communities with wildlife (especially elephants) and the elite bureaucrats who decided what was allowed in the forest. In the twelve years since, I've seen this pattern play out across India and beyond. None of my formal training prepared me for this, so I wrote a book to help conservation enthusiasts better understand the problems they seek to solve.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

NS: I believe wildlife conservation has been misrepresented as being primarily about biodiversity and ecosystem function. Those things matter, and many academics do think that the number of species that survive is what conservation is all about. But most people care about wildlife because we sense that animals' lives matter, or because it brings us joy when our paths intersect with those of other thinking, feeling beings. Conservation is really about enriching all our lives, human and non-human.

article continues after advertisement

The Elephant Jungle shows how wildlife has value even for people struggling to survive like Netra and his community—and that this value comes from animals both as species and as sentient individuals. By telling this story, I hope to demonstrate not just why conservation is hard and morally complex, but what it's really about.

Source: Books of Change/with permission.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

NS: My primary interest is to reach people dedicating something to conservation: students aspiring to become conservationists, policy makers who want to foster sustainable and equitable development, donors developing a theory of change for wildlife conservation. We need more population-level awareness of the true costs and benefits of international wildlife conservation.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

NS: The Elephant Jungle describes the typical evolution of a protected area in the Global South, showing how elites have disregarded local people. Buxa Tiger Reserve was declared without consulting the people who already lived there or offering any way to offset the forest resources they were being deprived of. This inequitable history means we have to address a legacy of injustice to make conservation fair.

A related theme is trade-offs. Most of us who care about conservation also want social justice for our fellow humans, but without careful thought, one can come at the expense of the other. Fortress conservation can mean the most marginalized people lose access to resources they depend on. Unfettered access to forest resources can fuel local development, but also destroy crucial habitat. The book explores what it means to strike a balance and find win-wins.

Because these problems are so complicated, the book is also about humility. I started off in Buxa assuming the disappearing forest and tigers were signs of mismanagement. I hope readers experience the same transformation I did: I got a better idea of what may be possible, and saw clear opportunities for improvement, but ultimately had to admit I didn't know what would really work, or even if the problem was solvable.

article continues after advertisement

Finally, Buxa serves as a microcosm for one of the great miracles of conservation: how is the most populous region in human history also still home to the world's largest populations of tigers, Asian elephants, Asiatic lions, one-horned rhinos, and other globally important species? The Elephant Jungle shows how people's attitudes toward animals may be key. When the prevailing culture acknowledges that individual animals can feel joy and suffer, and may have some entitlement to seek resources even when it's inconvenient for humans, it may leave just enough space for survival—even amid plenty of harm and violence.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

NS: I don't know of many other narrative non-fiction books that focus on the lives of the humans who live alongside wildlife. Conservation books often focus on species at large or place a well-educated conservationist at the center of the story. I've seen fiction books and movies explore the realities of living alongside wildlife, but I wasn't satisfied with their realism. The Elephant Jungle sits at the intersection of non-fiction, conservation writing, and creative narrative.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about the fascinating lives of elephants and how important it is to coexist with them and treat them with more respect and dignity?

NS: People broadly love elephants and see them as worthy of moral consideration. What's forestalling successful elephant conservation is the lack of sophistication and accountability in conservation institutions. The general public would be shocked by how little of the funds donated to large international NGOs actually goes to elephant conservation.

My hope is that The Elephant Jungle contributes to the conservation community's collective capacity for critical thinking. It took decades for society to start holding development and humanitarian organizations accountable for results. I expect reforming conservation—which must serve many species, not just one—will take even longer.
